```{python}
import polars as pl 
import numpy as np
from lets_plot import *
import polars.selectors as cs
# add the additional libraries you need to import for ML here

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)

data_url = "https://byuidatascience.github.io/DS250-Course-Polars/Data/StarWars_with_emails.csv"
a = pl.Series(pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows=10, n_rows=1, has_header=False, encoding='utf8-lossy').row(0))
a[2] = "seen_any"
a = (
  a.str.replace(r".+seen.+", "seen_")
   .str.replace(r".+rank.+", "rank_")
   .str.replace(r"(.+favorably.+)", "fav_")
   .fill_null(strategy="forward")
   .str.replace("\uFFFD+", "")
   .str.strip_chars()
   .str.to_lowercase()
   .str.replace_all(" ", "_")
   .str.replace(r"location(.+)", "location")
)
a[3] = "star_wars_fan"
a[30] = "who_shot_first"
a[31] = "know_expanded_universe"
a[32] = "expanded_universe_fan"
a[33] = "star_trek_fan"

b = pl.Series(pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows=11, n_rows=1, has_header=False, encoding='utf8-lossy').row(0))
b = (
  b.str.replace(r"Star Wars: (Episode \w+) .+", "${1}")
   .str.replace("Response", "")
   .str.replace_all(" ", "_")
   .fill_null("")
   .str.strip_chars()
)

new_names = (a + b).to_list()
df = pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows=12, has_header=False, new_columns=new_names)

# Filter to the 835 respondents who have seen at least one film
df_seen = df.filter(
    pl.any_horizontal(cs.starts_with("seen_Episode").is_not_null())
)
```

## QUESTION 1

Validate that the data provided lines up with the article by recreating 2 of the visuals from the article.

To validate that the dataset on GitHub matches the data behind the FiveThirtyEight
article, I recreated two of the article's charts: "Which 'Star Wars' Movies Have
You Seen?" and "What's the Best 'Star Wars' Movie?". If the percentages in my
recreations match the published charts, we can be confident the dataset is the
same one used for the story.

```{python}

titles = {
    "Episode_I":   "The Phantom Menace",
    "Episode_II":  "Attack of the Clones",
    "Episode_III": "Revenge of the Sith",
    "Episode_IV":  "A New Hope",
    "Episode_V":   "The Empire Strikes Back",
    "Episode_VI":  "Return of the Jedi",
}
order = list(titles.values())


fivethirtyeight_theme = (
    theme_minimal()
    + theme(
        axis_text_x=element_blank(),
        axis_ticks=element_blank(),
        panel_grid=element_blank(),
        plot_title=element_text(face="bold", size=16),
        plot_subtitle=element_text(size=12),
        plot_background=element_rect(fill="#f0f0f0"),
        panel_background=element_rect(fill="#f0f0f0"),
    )
)
```

### Visual 1: Which 'Star Wars' Movies Have You Seen?

The article reports, for the 835 respondents who have seen at least one film,
the percentage that has seen each of the six movies. Each `seen_Episode_*`
column contains the movie title if the person marked it and null otherwise, so
counting non-null values per column and dividing by 835 reproduces the chart.
The wide seen-columns are unpivoted into a long (movie, count) table for
plotting.

```{python}
# Count how many respondents saw each movie, then convert to percent of 835
seen_long = (
    df_seen
    .select(cs.starts_with("seen_Episode").is_not_null().cast(pl.Int32))
    .sum()                                            # one row of counts
    .unpivot(variable_name="movie", value_name="n")   # wide -> long
    .with_columns(
        pl.col("movie").str.replace("seen_", "").replace_strict(titles).alias("title"),
        (pl.col("n") / df_seen.height * 100).round(0).cast(pl.Int32).alias("pct"),
    )
)

(
    ggplot(seen_long, aes(x="title", y="pct"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="#008fd5", width=0.7)
    + geom_text(aes(label="pct"), nudge_y=4, size=7)
    + coord_flip()
    + scale_x_discrete(limits=order[::-1])  # Episode I on top, VI on bottom
    + labs(
        title="Which 'Star Wars' Movies Have You Seen?",
        subtitle=f"Of {df_seen.height} respondents who have seen any film",
        x="", y="",
    )
    + fivethirtyeight_theme
    + ggsize(700, 400)
)
```

The recreated percentages (roughly 80, 68, 66, 73, 91, and 88 percent for
Episodes I through VI) match the values printed on the bars in the article's
chart, with The Empire Strikes Back as the most-seen film. This confirms the
seen-columns in the dataset line up with the published story.

### Visual 2: What's the Best 'Star Wars' Movie?

The article's "best movie" chart is restricted to respondents who have seen all
six films, and shows the percentage that ranked each movie as their number 1.
I first filter to people with all six seen-columns populated, then unpivot the
six `rank_*` columns into a long table and keep only the rank-1 votes.

```{python}
# Respondents who saw all six films (the article reports 471)
saw_all = df_seen.filter(
    pl.all_horizontal(cs.starts_with("seen_Episode").is_not_null())
)

# Unpivot the rank columns and keep each person's #1 pick
best_long = (
    saw_all
    .select(cs.starts_with("rank_"))
    .unpivot(variable_name="movie", value_name="rank")
    .filter(pl.col("rank") == 1)
    .group_by("movie")
    .agg(pl.len().alias("n"))
    .with_columns(
        pl.col("movie").str.replace("rank_", "").replace_strict(titles).alias("title"),
        (pl.col("n") / saw_all.height * 100).round(0).cast(pl.Int32).alias("pct"),
    )
)

(
    ggplot(best_long, aes(x="title", y="pct"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="#008fd5", width=0.7)
    + geom_text(aes(label="pct"), nudge_y=2, size=7)
    + coord_flip()
    + scale_x_discrete(limits=order[::-1])
    + labs(
        title="What's the Best 'Star Wars' Movie?",
        subtitle=f"Of {saw_all.height} respondents who have seen all six films",
        x="", y="",
    )
    + fivethirtyeight_theme
    + ggsize(700, 400)
)
```

The filter returns 471 respondents, the same denominator the article reports,
and The Empire Strikes Back is the winner at roughly 36 percent, matching the
published chart. With both recreations agreeing with the article, the dataset
is validated: the values on GitHub are the same values behind the
FiveThirtyEight story, and the client can trust the rest of the analysis built
on this data.
